newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Sarkozy gives prescription for reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: France's Sarkozy gives prescription for reshuffle.

text.p: France's ex-budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, tipped as a returnee in a possible government reshuffle, said on Sunday that any team change should comprise changes in policy.

Sarkozy told RTL radio that he had met fellow-Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe for two hours of talks and told him that the objectives of cleaning up finances and a European single currency should be maintained.

"If there were to be a reshuffle, it should correspond to a new departure for the government, with the same objectives. It should go faster on some issues, slower on others. It is not enough to simply change people," Sarkozy said.

"Let's discuss things, let's draw up what should be the poilcy followed by France...We should maintain our monetary policy, speed up fiscal policy, and slow down our thinking on social legislation," Sarkozy said.

Juppe, whose popularity has tumbled because of record unemployment of 12.6 percent and budget austerity to help France qualify for a single European currency from 1999, has faced widening criticism of his rule.
Last week, a source at President Jacques Chirac's office said rumours of an imminent change had no foundation. "If there is a reshuffle, it would probably be at the start of 1997," the source said.
Asked whether Juppe should remain prime minister in a reshuffle, Sarkozy answered: "The president maintains his confidence in his prime minister. Is he right to do so? Events will tell."

Another former minister, Simone Veil of the UDF, junior partner in the ruling coalition, told Europe-1 radio that a reshuffle would not change much because the priority was not to change individuals but to reform institutions.

She pointed to a seven-day-old strike by truckers, who are blockading several towns and petrol depots, as evidence "that the problem with our constitution is that it does not sufficiently encourage concert and dialogue".
Sarkozy lambasted former President Valery Giscard d'Estaing for proposing a devaluation of the franc to breathe life into the economy and create jobs.

"If we don't want the single currency to happen, if we want European union to explose, if we want to return to the sterile debate between pro- and anti-Maastricht people, that's the right way to go about it," Sarkozy said.
"The consequences of (Giscard D'Estaing's appeal) were negative for the solidity of our currency, and for the solidity of the Franco-German couple. That's not a good start," he added.

Senate speaker Rene Monory, a member of the centrist UDF party which is the junior partner in France's ruling coalition, has called for a cabinet reshuffle that would leave Juppe in place but bring in committed pro-Europeans.
Monory said he believed changing prime ministers would not be useful because whoever headed the government would be unpopular due to France's austerity policies.
